To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

90% of anaesthetic trainees report feeling fatigued, 60% of anaesthetic consultants report feeling tired, 40% report feeling exhausted, 50% of trainees have had to take time off work because of fatigue, and only 10% of trainees and consultants report that their employers have taken action to address the problem.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how junior doctors in the NHS are affected by the pressures of their working lives.
the effects of fatigue in anaesthetic trainees, but we believe the issues are relevant to the whole of the NHS, and the wider society.
fatigue and its effects on junior doctors in anaesthetic training.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the NHS is not a healthy place to be working in at the moment, especially as a junior doctor.
the NHS is in a state of fatigue crisis.
the findings from this study suggest that the NHS is not fit for purpose.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we found that fatigue is a common problem for junior anaesthetists, that it has a significant impact on their personal and professional lives, that there are few strategies in place to address it and that there is a significant lack of knowledge and awareness of fatigue within our specialty and in the NHS as a whole.
the majority of anaesthetic trainees in the UK experience fatigue, with 50% of those experiencing fatigue feeling that it affects their clinical decision making.
the NHS is not currently a safe place to work.

the problem of fatigue is not confined to the operating room, or the intensive care unit, or the Emergency Department.
the NHS has a serious fatigue problem, and we need to start talking about it.
fatigue is a significant issue for anaesthetic trainees, and that it is a problem which has been largely ignored.
